newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rwandan Hutus kill three in attack on Zaire rebels.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan Hutus kill three in attack on Zaire rebels.

text.p: At least three people were killed in an attack by armed Rwandan Hutus on a village held by Zairean rebels in renewed violence, witnesses said on Friday.

They said two civilians and a rebel soldier were killed at the village of Mushaki in the steep hills 40 km (25 miles) west of Goma, the biggest town held by the rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL).
The Alliance is led by Laurent Kabila, a longtime opponent of Zairean President Mobutu Sese.
"The village was attacked yesterday, and again this morning, which was when the people were killed," said the rebel officer commanding the checkpoint at Mushaki, who would not be named.
Pointing towards nearby hills he said: "the Interahamwe (Rwandans) are just along the road over there and we are waiting for them to come out."

The attack is the latest incident in an upsurge of violence in the ethnic-strife torn region west of Goma where remnants of the Hutu former Rwandan army have clashed sporadically with rebels fighting to topple Zaire's president Mobutu Sese Seko with backing from Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army.
Villagers fleeing Mushaki reported seeing armed men attacking at dawn on Friday with guns and machetes and said that rebel fighters had retreated before returning later in the morning.

"This is the third time we have been forced to run away in the past year," said Kanumuyeri Nyirasebura, a Tutsi who had only spent two weeks in Mushaki since returning from the last time she had fled with her children.

The unhappy ethnic mix of the region, known as Masisi after its largest town, has given it little peace in recent years as thousands have died in clashes between Hutus, Tutsis, Hundes and other local ethnic groups.
The flames of hatred were fanned still further by the arrival nearby in 1994 of at least 700,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees who had fled after the genocide of hundreds of thousands of Tutsis.

Although the bulk of the refugees returned home after the arrival of the Zairean rebels in November some pockets of the former army and "interahamwe" militias remain trapped inside Zaire after fleeing to the west.
Among the scattered farming hamlets of the region the Rwandans can find temporary refuge among a Zairean Hutu population that dominates some parts of Masisi.

Kabila on Thursday told Reuters that groups of Rwandans driven from Walikale, 130 km (85 miles) west of Goma had been crossing the Masisi region and heading into the thick forests which approach the Rwandan border.

"We have a little bit of trouble from the Interahamwe who we chased from Walikale and who are now attacking us to try and find a safe road to somewhere they can be helped by friends like Mobutu and the French," Kabila said.
Mobutu was more than close to Juvenal Habiyarimana, the former Rwandan Hutu president whose death in a plane crash triggered the 1994 massacres in Rwanda.

Rich in mineral deposits but impoverished after years of mismanagement and corruption Zaire faces its worst crisis in decades, with Kabila's rebels controlling a 600 km (400 miles) swathe of territory along the border with Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi.
